title: An install-time hook runs with the developer's privileges before any review, anchored on a publish token
index_line: T-0058 · EXEC · phished npm token publishes four versions whose postinstall drops and runs a payload · shell/node · corroborated
invariant_violated: Adding a dependency is treated as a supply decision reviewed once, at the version you read. But a package's install script executes on the developer's machine and in CI at `npm install`, with their user's rights and their environment's secrets — before any import, any test, any review. And the only thing standing between an attacker and publishing is a token that phishes like any other credential.

mechanism.does: the attacker obtains the maintainer's package-registry token by phishing (a fake login page, not a code exploit)
they publish versions of a legitimately popular package that include a lifecycle hook script alongside unchanged library code
a developer or CI job installs or updates the package, and the package manager runs the hook as part of installation
the hook drops and starts a payload on the host, with the installing user's privileges and environment
the payload runs a command on the developer's machine or build runner

source.env.value: the dependency manifest plus its resolved versions — the input is a package coordinate, not a request

delegate.tool.value: the package manager's lifecycle hook (postinstall/prepare), which exists to run arbitrary code at install time

guard.signature.value: provenance and publish authentication: 2FA, attestations, lockfile integrity. The publish token is the anchor that failed

sink.exec.shell.value: the hook's interpreter, running in the developer's or runner's context

preconditions.expr: the package manager runs lifecycle scripts from dependencies by default
the project installs or updates the affected packages, directly or transitively
the host can run the payload (the known variant targets Windows

success: an unexpected child process or outbound connection during install, before any application code runs
a new binary or script appears in a cache, temp or package directory outside the project
the lockfile resolves to a version whose published tarball differs from the repository tag
failure_like: the environment disables lifecycle scripts, or pins integrity and refuses the new versions
the platform is one the payload does not target (the known variant was Windows-only)
false_positive: a legitimate package that always had a postinstall step — compare against the previous version's manifest
an install-time network call from a registry mirror, not from the package

hazards: the registry token is the trust anchor and it is phishable; publish-side 2FA and provenance attestations are the only real controls
install-time code runs before your dependency policy has a chance to look at the code — review the manifest, not just the source
this is the dependency-install sibling of T-0038 (a mutable CI tag): both are 'the reference moved and something ran'
CI is the higher-value target: a runner holds deploy credentials, and install happens on every build
non_transfers: environments that install with scripts disabled and run only vetted build steps
registries that enforce provenance attestations tied to a verified identity
